body_html:
Peak weather season in Dallas runs from roughly March through June, when warm Gulf moisture meets dry western air and fuels hail, tornadoes, damaging winds and flash flooding. April and May are usually the most active months. A smaller secondary storm season often returns in October and November, so Dallas property owners should prepare twice a year.

When is peak weather season in Dallas?

Dallas sits in one of the most active severe-weather corridors in the country. Each spring, the jet stream dips over the southern Plains, warm humid air flows north from the Gulf of Mexico, and dry air from West Texas pushes in behind it. Where those air masses collide, supercell thunderstorms form fast and can produce large hail and tornadoes.

That pattern makes spring the core of peak weather season in Dallas. Storms can show up as early as February, but activity usually ramps up in March, peaks in April and May, and tapers through June as summer heat caps the atmosphere.

Dallas weather calendar at a glance

MonthsTypical conditionsPrimary property risks
January–FebruaryCool, occasional arctic frontsFreezes, burst pipes, ice, early hail
March–JuneWarm, humid, unstableHail, tornadoes, straight-line winds, flash flooding
July–SeptemberHot and mostly dryHeat stress on roofs, drought, isolated storms
October–NovemberTransitional frontsSecondary hail and wind events, occasional tornadoes
DecemberMild to coolGenerally lower risk, occasional freezes

The National Weather Service Fort Worth/Dallas forecast office issues local watches and warnings and is the best place to follow active weather in North Texas.

When is hail season in Texas?

Hail season in Texas generally runs from March through June, with the highest activity in April and May for most of the state. Timing shifts by region:

  • Central and North Texas, including Dallas, Fort Worth, Austin and Waco, typically see peak hail in April and May.
  • The Panhandle and West Texas, including Amarillo, Lubbock and Midland, often stay active later, into May and June.
  • South Texas and the Gulf Coast get hail too, though tropical systems and flooding are the bigger seasonal concern there.

Fall can bring a second round of hail across North Texas when strong cold fronts arrive in October and November. Fewer storms occur then, but they can still be damaging.

When does it hail? The time of day matters

Most Texas hailstorms form in the late afternoon and evening, when daytime heating has made the atmosphere most unstable. Storms can continue overnight, especially when a line of storms moves east from West Texas. That timing means many homeowners discover damage the next morning, which is why a quick photo walk-around after any overnight storm is a good habit.

How big does hail have to be to damage a roof?

The National Weather Service classifies hail one inch in diameter (about the size of a quarter) or larger as severe. Hail that size can bruise asphalt shingles, crack older or brittle roofing and dent gutters, vents and metal. Smaller hail can still cause damage when it is driven by strong wind or falls on aging materials.

Size is not the only factor. Hail density, wind speed, the age and type of your roof and how long the storm lasts all affect how much damage you get. Two houses on the same street can have very different results, which is why each roof deserves its own inspection.

When is tornado season in Dallas?

Tornado season in Dallas overlaps with hail season. The highest risk is generally March through June, peaking in April and May. North Texas also has a secondary tornado season in the fall. The October 2019 tornado that struck north Dallas is a reminder that fall storms can be just as destructive as spring ones.

Tornado damage is often severe and concentrated: roofs torn off, walls collapsed, windows blown out and debris impact across a neighborhood. Claims tend to be large and complex. Our guide to tornado damage insurance explains how those claims work.

Before tornado season, pick an interior room on the lowest floor as your shelter, keep a weather radio or phone alerts turned on, and store copies of your policy and home inventory somewhere you can reach from any device. If a tornado damages your home, those records will speed up every step of the claim.

Why Dallas storms are so costly for property owners

Dallas-Fort Worth combines frequent severe weather with a huge, growing footprint of homes and commercial buildings. When a hailstorm crosses the Metroplex, it can damage thousands of roofs in a single afternoon. That creates three challenges for owners:

  1. Demand surges. Roofers, adjusters and suppliers get booked up quickly after big storms.
  2. Hidden damage. Hail bruises shingles and dents metal in ways that are hard to see from the ground and may leak weeks later.
  3. Disputes over cause and age. Carriers may attribute damage to wear, prior storms or poor installation rather than the most recent event.

Typical damage patterns after peak season storms

  • Shingles cracked, bruised or missing granules from hail
  • Siding, gutters and window screens dented or punctured
  • HVAC condenser fins crushed
  • Roof leaks that appear days or weeks after impact
  • Fence, garage door and soft-metal damage
  • Fallen limbs and wind-lifted shingles

For more on how timing affects claims, read how peak weather season affects roof damage claims in Dallas.

How to prepare your property before peak weather season

The best time to prepare is late winter, before the first big spring storm. This checklist covers the essentials:

  1. Get a roof inspection in January or February. Fix lifted flashing, loose shingles and worn sealant now so you can separate new storm damage from old issues later.
  2. Document your property's condition. Take date-stamped photos and video of your roof, siding, windows, HVAC units and interior ceilings. Before-photos are some of the strongest evidence in a claim.
  3. Trim trees hanging over the roof, driveway or power lines.
  4. Clean gutters and downspouts so heavy rain drains away from the foundation and fascia.
  5. Secure outdoor items like patio furniture, grills and trampolines that become projectiles in high wind.
  6. Plan for vehicles. Clear garage space so cars can be covered when hail is forecast.
  7. Know your policy, especially your wind/hail deductible and any roof endorsements.
Tip: Store your pre-season photos in the cloud with the date in the file name. If you ever need to prove a roof was in good shape before a storm, you will have it in seconds.

Our claim documentation checklist lists every photo and record worth collecting before and after a storm.

Check your insurance before storm season starts

Many Dallas homeowners only read their policy after a storm. Reading it in February is far less stressful. Focus on these items:

Policy itemWhat to look for
Wind/hail deductibleOften a percentage of dwelling coverage, such as 1% or 2%
Roof coverageWhether older roofs are paid at actual cash value or on a schedule
Cosmetic damage exclusionWhether dents to metal roofing or siding are excluded
Dwelling limitWhether it reflects today's rebuild cost
Appraisal clauseHow disputes over the amount of loss are resolved

A percentage deductible can be thousands of dollars. Learn why in why peak season matters to your insurance deductible in Dallas.

How peak weather season in Dallas affects commercial properties

Peak weather season in Dallas hits commercial owners hard. Large flat and low-slope roofs on warehouses, retail centers, apartment complexes and churches present a huge target for hail, and damage to membranes, insulation and rooftop units is often invisible from the ground.

  • Inspect rooftop equipment such as HVAC units, skylights and drains before spring.
  • Document roof condition with photos, core samples or moisture surveys when practical.
  • Review tenant responsibilities in leases so everyone knows who reports and repairs what.
  • Know your commercial deductible, which may be a percentage of the building's insured value.

Because commercial claims involve more square footage and more components, small scope differences turn into large dollar differences. A careful baseline before peak weather season in Dallas makes the claim far easier to support afterward.

What to do after a Dallas storm damages your property

  1. Stay safe. Avoid downed lines and do not climb onto a wet or damaged roof.
  2. Photograph everything before cleanup, including hail on the ground next to a coin or ruler for scale.
  3. Prevent further damage with tarps or board-up, and keep receipts.
  4. Report the claim promptly. Texas insurers generally must acknowledge a claim within 15 days of notice under Tex. Ins. Code ch. 542.
  5. Get an independent inspection and estimate so you can compare it with the carrier's.
  6. Review the carrier's estimate line by line for missing items like flashing, vents, gutters and code upgrades.

Peak season brings predictable disagreements over hail versus wear, repair versus replacement and pricing. We break those down in common insurance disputes during peak weather in Dallas.

Next steps if your storm claim comes up short

If the carrier accepts your claim but the payment does not cover the real repair cost, most Texas property policies include an appraisal clause. Each side names an appraiser, and an umpire resolves remaining differences over the amount of loss. It is often faster and less expensive than litigation. faqs.q: What month has the most hail in Texas?
faqs.a: For most of Texas, including Dallas-Fort Worth and Central Texas, April and May are typically the most active hail months. The Panhandle and West Texas often stay active into June. Hail can also occur in fall when strong cold fronts move through, so property owners should stay alert outside the spring peak as well.

faqs.q: Is there a fall storm season in Dallas?
faqs.a: Yes. North Texas often sees a secondary severe-weather season in October and November as strong cold fronts collide with lingering warm, humid air. Fall storms are less frequent than spring storms but can still produce damaging hail, high winds and tornadoes, as the October 2019 north Dallas tornado showed.

faqs.q: How long after a hailstorm can I file a claim in Texas?
faqs.a: Policies generally require prompt notice, so report storm damage as soon as reasonably possible. Some Texas policies also set specific time limits for filing wind and hail claims, and lawsuits over weather claims have their own deadlines and pre-suit notice rules. Check your policy and report early rather than waiting.

faqs.q: Should I get my roof inspected before storm season?
faqs.a: Yes. A pre-season inspection in late winter lets you fix existing issues and gives you a documented baseline of your roof's condition. That record helps separate new storm damage from prior wear, which is one of the most common points of dispute in Dallas hail claims.

faqs.q: Does homeowners insurance cover hail damage in Dallas?
faqs.a: Most Texas homeowners policies cover hail damage to the structure, subject to your wind/hail deductible. Some policies limit coverage with cosmetic damage exclusions or pay older roofs at actual cash value. Review your declarations page and endorsements so you know what to expect before a storm hits.
